name: Poly-MVA

card.summary: A palladium-lipoic acid liquid supplement promoted for cellular energy and anti-aging support, which proponents link to vitality and healthier-looking aging.
card.note: Marketed for cancer and other illnesses; discuss with a clinician, especially during cancer treatment.

quick.overview:
Poly-MVA is a red-brown liquid dietary supplement containing a palladium-alpha-lipoic acid complex with B vitamins, amino acids and minerals such as molybdenum, rhodium and ruthenium. It was created by Merrill Garnett and is sold mainly for energy, mitochondrial support and as a complementary product in cancer care.

In longevity circles it is discussed as an antioxidant and cellular-energy supplement, the idea being better recovery and slower age-related decline. The published research is mostly laboratory and rodent work, plus a small open-label registration in ALS fatigue.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth as a liquid, often alongside other supplements. Costs are high; a 2004 report put a year's supply at US$19,800.
quick.risks: Concern has been raised that antioxidant-type supplements could interfere with conventional cancer therapy. Palladium and the formula's other metals have limited human safety data.

lead: Poly-MVA, also called Lipoic Acid Mineral Complex, is a dietary supplement built around a palladium-alpha-lipoic acid complex, combined with B vitamins, amino acids and trace minerals. It was developed by Merrill Garnett, a former dentist turned biochemist.[1]

Within longevity and wellness communities it is described as supporting mitochondrial energy and antioxidant defenses, the pathway by which supporters hope for more energy, recovery and healthier-looking aging. Manufacturers and users have also promoted it for cancer and other diseases, largely on testimonials.[1]

Published studies are mainly in cells and rodents, reporting effects on cardiac mitochondrial enzymes in aged rats, radioprotection in mice, and reduced skin papilloma formation in a chemical-carcinogenesis model.[2][3][4][5] One open-label phase 1 study of fatigue in people with ALS has been registered.[6]

chain: Claimed support of mitochondrial energy and antioxidant status
Possible gains in energy and recovery (claimed)
angle.text: Proponents present it as a cellular-energy supplement for healthier aging. Any link to appearance runs through general vitality and recovery rather than a direct effect on skin or features.

paras: The name stands for minerals, vitamins and amino acids; listed ingredients include lipoic acid, acetylcysteine, palladium and B vitamins.[1] It is promoted for conditions including cancer and HIV/AIDS, with testimonials as the main support, and Wikipedia describes it as an unproven alternative cancer treatment, noting concern about interference with standard treatment.[1]

In aged rats, Poly-MVA raised activity of Krebs cycle dehydrogenases and respiratory complexes in heart tissue and altered mitochondrial antioxidant enzymes.[4][5] In mice it enhanced the antitumor effect of radiation and protected blood DNA and platelets,[2][7] and attenuated chemically induced skin papillomas.[3] In gerbils it was studied against ischemic cell death,[8] and in a rat model a late-administered formulation changed cardiac mitochondria without altering functional or structural radiation heart disease.[9] A voltammetry and microscopy study reported that the complex interacts with DNA without causing oxidative damage.[10]

A phase 1 open-label study of Poly-MVA for ALS fatigue, with 12 participants, was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov in 2020 and is listed as completed.[6] No published human trials examine appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Experimental Neurology gerbil ischemia study published; yearly cost reported at US$19,800.[1][8]
